claim: More than a third of neurons in mouse V1 are color-opponent in their receptive field center.
source: we found that more than a third of neurons in mouse V1 are color-opponent in their receptive field center
evidence: Supported by experimental data from large-scale neuronal recordings using luminance and color noise stimulus

claim: The receptive field surround of mouse V1 neurons predominantly captures luminance contrast.
source: the receptive field surround predominantly captures luminance contrast
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing surround responses primarily encode luminance information

claim: Color-opponency is especially pronounced in posterior V1 that encodes the sky.
source: color-opponency is especially pronounced in posterior V1 that encodes the sky
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing posterior and anterior V1 recordings

claim: The asymmetry in color representations across cortex can be explained by an uneven distribution of green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types.
source: the asymmetry in color representations across cortex can be explained by an uneven distribution of green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types that are represented in the upper visual field
evidence: Supported by unsupervised clustering analysis showing distribution of response types

claim: Green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types are represented in the upper visual field.
source: green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types that are represented in the upper visual field
evidence: Supported by experimental data from posterior V1 recordings

claim: Green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types may enhance the detection of 'predatory'-like dark UV-objects in noisy daylight scenes.
source: green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types may enhance the detection of 'predatory'-like dark UV-objects in noisy daylight scenes
evidence: Supported by computational modeling with natural scene-inspired parametric stimuli

claim: Mice are dichromatic and have two cone photoreceptor types expressing UV- and green-sensitive S- and M-opsin.
source: Like most mammals, mice are dichromatic and have two cone photoreceptor types, expressing ultraviolet (UV)- and green-sensitive S- and M-opsin (Szél et al., 1992), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature

claim: Mice have one type of rod photoreceptor which is green-sensitive.
source: In addition, they have one type of rod photoreceptor which is green-sensitive.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: UV- and green-sensitive cone photoreceptors predominantly sample the upper and lower visual field, respectively, through an uneven opsin distribution across the retina.
source: Importantly, UV- and green-sensitive cone photoreceptors predominantly sample the upper and lower visual field, respectively, through an uneven opsin distribution across the retina (Szél et al., 1992; Baden et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Mice can discriminate different colors.
source: Behavioral studies have demonstrated that mice can discriminate different colors (Jacobs et al., 2004), at least in the upper visual field (Denman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies

claim: Mice can discriminate different colors at least in the upper visual field.
source: Behavioral studies have demonstrated that mice can discriminate different colors (Jacobs et al., 2004), at least in the upper visual field (Denman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to behavioral study

claim: 33.1% of V1 neurons preferred color-opponent stimuli.
source: Nevertheless, a substantial fraction of neurons (33.1%) preferred color-opponent stimuli and scattered along the off-diagonal in the upper left and lower right quadrants, especially for the RF center.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data

claim: The luminance axis captured 82% of the variance of stimulus sensitivity for the RF surround.
source: The luminance axis captured the major part of the variance of stimulus sensitivity for the RF surround (82%)
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of experimental data

claim: The luminance axis explained 67% of the variance for the RF center.
source: while it explained less of the variance for the RF center (67%)
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of experimental data

claim: One-third (33%) of the variance within the tested stimulus sensitivity space of the RF center was explained by the color axis.
source: As a result, one-third (33%) of the variance within the tested stimulus sensitivity space of the RF center was explained by the color axis.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of experimental data

claim: The majority of neurons showed negatively correlated center and surround ETAs for both the UV and green channels.
source: First, the majority of neurons showed negatively correlated center and surround ETAs for both the UV and green channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: Neurons recorded in posterior and anterior V1 preferred UV and green stimuli, respectively.
source: Second, neurons recorded in posterior and anterior V1 preferred UV and green stimuli (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e, f), respectively, in line with the distribution of cone opsins across the retina (Szél et al., 1992; Baden et al., 2013) and previous cortical work (Rhim et al., 2017; Franke et al., 2022; Aihara et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to previous work

claim: The asymmetry in color preference was less pronounced for the surround.
source: This asymmetry in color preference was less pronounced for the surround (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e, f), as has been reported for retinal neurons in mice (Szatko et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to previous work

claim: The pronounced center color-opponency in V1 neurons cannot be solely attributed to the color-opponency present in the RF center of retinal ganglion cells.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the pronounced center color-opponency in V1 neurons cannot be solely attributed to the color-opponency present in the RF center of retinal ganglion cells.
evidence: Supported by comparison of V1 and retinal data

claim: The pronounced center color-opponency in V1 likely depends on the activation of both the center and surround of retinal neurons.
source: It likely depends on the activation of both the center and surround of retinal neurons, as well as a potential remapping of retinal center and surround RFs in downstream processing stages.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of V1 and retinal data

claim: The neuronal representation of color in mouse visual cortex greatly decreases when reducing ambient light levels.
source: The neuronal representation of color greatly decreased when reducing ambient light levels
evidence: Supported by experimental data at different light levels

claim: Decreasing ambient light levels resulted in a reduction of UV sensitivity in posterior V1 neurons.
source: Indeed, decreasing ambient light levels resulted in a reduction of UV sensitivity in posterior V1 neurons (Figure 3a)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figure

claim: The neuronal representation of color in mouse visual cortex is strongest for photopic light levels that predominantly drive cone photoreceptors.
source: our results demonstrate that the neuronal representation of color in mouse visual cortex greatly depends on ambient light levels, and is strongest for photopic light levels that predominantly drive cone photoreceptors
evidence: Supported by experimental data at different light levels

claim: The color axis explained 39% of the variance in the upper visual field.
source: It captured 39% of the variance in the upper visual field and only 19% of the variance in the lower visual field.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of experimental data

claim: The color axis explained 19% of the variance in the lower visual field.
source: It captured 39% of the variance in the upper visual field and only 19% of the variance in the lower visual field.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of experimental data

claim: The discriminability of stimulus color was significantly higher when using the responses of posterior V1 neurons for decoding.
source: In line with this, the discriminability of stimulus color was significantly higher when using the responses of posterior V1 neurons for decoding (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis of experimental data

claim: Color contrast in scenes from the mouse's natural environment is enriched in the upper visual field.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that color contrast in scenes from the mouse's natural environment is enriched in the upper visual field (Figure 4a; Qiu et al., 2021; Abballe and Asari, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The mean assignment accuracy of generated ground-truth labels was 89.2% (±6%).
source: The mean assignment accuracy of generated ground-truth labels was 89.2% (±6%)
evidence: Supported by validation of clustering analysis

claim: All response types were present in all mice.
source: all response types were present in all mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data across animals

claim: Approximately half of the response types were sensitive to luminance contrast.
source: Approximately half of the response types were sensitive to luminance contrast (types 1–8)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis of experimental data

claim: Response types with green-Off/UV-On color-opponency were uniformly spread across the anterior-posterior axis of mouse V1.
source: Interestingly, response types with green-Off/UV-On color-opponency were also uniformly spread across the anterior-posterior axis of mouse V1
evidence: Supported by analysis of response type distribution

claim: Response types with a green-On/UV-Off color-opponency were almost exclusively confined to posterior V1.
source: To our surprise, response types with a green-On/UV-Off color-opponency were almost exclusively confined to posterior V1.
evidence: Supported by analysis of response type distribution

claim: The color axis explained 73% of ETA variance for the response types enriched in posterior cortex.
source: As a result of this, the color axis explained 73% of ETA variance for the response types enriched in posterior cortex
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of response types

claim: The color axis explained 17% of ETA variance for the anterior-enriched response types.
source: while it explained only 17% for the anterior-enriched response types
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of response types

claim: Green-On/UV-Off response types were the two best performing types for decoding dark objects in noisy scenes.
source: While all Off-center response types sensitive to luminance contrast could decode the dark object, the two best performing types corresponded to the green-On/UV-Off response types enriched in posterior V1 (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling and decoding analysis

claim: The good performance of green-On/UV-Off types was due to the absence of responses to the noise scenes, rather than strong responses to the object scenes per se.
source: Interestingly, the reason for their good performance was the absence of responses to the noise scenes, rather than strong responses to the object scenes per se (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by computational modeling analysis

claim: Color-opponency in mouse V1 is at least partially mediated by the comparison of cone photoreceptor signals.
source: Color-opponency in the RF center was strongest for photopic light levels largely activating cone photoreceptors and greatly decreased for mesopic light levels, suggesting that the observed color-opponency in V1 is at least partially mediated by the comparison of cone photoreceptor signals.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data at different light levels

claim: At the level of the mouse retina, color-opponency is largely mediated by center-surround interactions.
source: At the level of the mouse retina, color-opponency is largely mediated by center-surround interactions (Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Joesch and Meister, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Only a few retinal neurons exhibit color-opponency in their centers.
source: with only a few neurons exhibiting color-opponency in their centers (Hoefling et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The extensive and sophisticated color processing in the mouse LGN cannot be fully explained by the proposed retinal opponency mechanisms.
source: Similarly, a recent study concluded that the extensive and sophisticated color processing in the mouse LGN cannot be fully explained by the proposed retinal opponency mechanisms (Mouland et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: In primate species, a small number of distinct retinal cell types transmit color information to downstream visual areas.
source: In primates, physiological and anatomical evidence suggest that a small number of distinct retinal cell types transmit color information to downstream visual areas (reviewed in Thoreson and Dacey, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to review article

claim: In primates, the neuronal representation of color remains partially segregated from the representation of other visual features like form.
source: where the neuronal representation of color remains partially segregated from the representation of other visual features like form (Livingstone and Hubel, 1988; Zeki, 1978, but see Garg et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Color-sensitive neurons in primate primary and secondary visual cortex are enriched in the 'blob' and 'inter-stripe' regions, respectively.
source: For example, color-sensitive neurons in primary and secondary visual cortex are enriched in the so-called 'blob' (Hubel and Livingstone, 1987) and 'inter-stripe' regions (DeYoe and Van Essen, 1985), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In zebrafish, birds, Drosophila, and mice, a large number of retinal output types encode information about stimulus color.
source: In zebrafish, birds, Drosophila, and mice, a large number of retinal output types encode information about stimulus color (Seifert et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2020; Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: There is evidence for distributed processing of color in visual areas downstream to the retina in zebrafish, mice, Drosophila, and tree shrew.
source: In addition, there is evidence for distributed processing of color in visual areas downstream to the retina in zebrafish (Guggiana Nilo et al., 2021), mice (Rhim and Nauhaus, 2023; Mouland et al., 2021), Drosophila (Longden et al., 2023), and tree shrew (Johnson et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The UV wavelength range aids the detection of objects like prey, predators, and food by increasing their contrast.
source: For example, it has been shown that the UV wavelength range aids the detection of objects like prey, predators, and food (reviewed in Cronin and Bok, 2016) by increasing their contrast, as recently shown for leaf surface contrasts in forest environments (Tedore and Nilsson, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Different photoreceptor types sensitive to distinct wavelength bands did not evolve to support color discrimination, but instead to reduce lighting noise in the natural environment of early vertebrates.
source: Indeed, it is hypothesized that different photoreceptor types sensitive to distinct wavelength bands did not evolve to support color discrimination, but instead to reduce lighting noise in the natural environment of early vertebrates (discussed in Maximov, 2000; Kelber et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous discussions

claim: For 83% of cells, the spatial ETA exhibited an overlap with the center spot area of the color noise stimulus of more than 0.65.
source: For most cells (83%), the spatial ETA exhibited an overlap with the center spot area of the color noise stimulus of more than 0.65.
evidence: Supported by spatial RF mapping analysis

claim: The center size of 37.5 degrees visual angle in diameter is larger than the mean center RF size of mouse V1 neurons (26.2±4.6 degrees visual angle in diameter).
source: The center size of 37.5 degrees visual angle in diameter is larger than the mean center RF size of mouse V1 neurons (26.2±4.6 degrees visual angle in diameter).
evidence: Supported by RF size measurements

claim: At the level of the retinal output, the color axis explained only 12% of the variance in the tested sensitivity space for the RF center.
source: We found that at the level of the retinal output, the color axis explained only 12% of the variance in the tested sensitivity space for the RF center (10 degrees visual angle)
evidence: Supported by analysis of retinal ganglion cell data

claim: The low fraction of center color-opponent retinal ganglion cells is in line with a recent study that characterized RF properties of these neurons using natural movies.
source: The low fraction of center color-opponent retinal ganglion cells is in line with a recent study that characterized RF properties of these neurons using natural movies recorded in the mouse's natural environment (Hoefling et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Weak cone activation in low mesopic light levels is sufficient to extract color features from the visual input.
source: This suggests that weak cone activation in low mesopic light levels is sufficient to extract color features from the visual input.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data at low mesopic light levels

claim: Spectral contrast significantly differed between posterior and anterior neurons for both center and surround.
source: Spectral contrast significantly differed between posterior and anterior neurons, for both center (p<0.001, two-sided two-sample t-test) and surround (p<0.001, two-sided two-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Spectral contrast significantly differed between center and surround for both posterior and anterior neurons.
source: Spectral contrast significantly differed between center and surround, for both posterior (p<0.001, two-sided two-sample t-test) and anterior neurons (p<0.001, two-sided two-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: For luminance contrast, decoding discriminability was significantly different between center and surround for n=50 and n=100 neurons.
source: For luminance contrast, decoding discriminability was significantly different between center and surround for n=50 and n=100 neurons (t-test for unpaired data, p-value was adjusted for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: For color contrast, decoding discriminability was significantly different between center and surround for all numbers of neurons tested, except n=1 neuron.
source: For color contrast, decoding discriminability was significantly different between center and surround for all numbers of neurons tested, except n=1 neuron.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: Decoding discriminability of the center was not significantly different across light levels for n=500 neurons.
source: For n=500 neurons, decoding discriminability of the center was not significantly different across light levels (t-test for unpaired data, p-value was adjusted for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: The surround discriminability was significantly lower than the center for the photopic condition.
source: The surround discriminability was significantly lower than the center for the photopic condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: Decoding discriminability was significantly different between center and surround for all three light levels.
source: Decoding discriminability was significantly different between center and surround for all three light levels.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: Discriminability for the center was significantly different between photopic and mesopic conditions, but not between the two mesopic conditions.
source: In addition, discriminability for the center was significantly different between photopic and mesopic conditions, but not between the two mesopic conditions (t-test for unpaired data, p-value was adjusted for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: The decoding discriminability was significantly different between anterior and posterior neurons.
source: The decoding discriminability was significantly different between anterior and posterior neurons (t-test for unpaired data, p-value was adjusted for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: Decoding discriminability was significantly different between anterior- and posterior-enriched types for all numbers of neurons tested.
source: Decoding discriminability was significantly different between anterior- and posterior-enriched types for all numbers of neurons tested (t-test for unpaired data, p-value was adjusted for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding results

claim: Functional recordings were obtained from posterior and anterior V1, encoding the upper and lower visual field, respectively.
source: Functional recordings were obtained from posterior and anterior V1 (Figure 1c), encoding the upper and lower visual field (Schuett et al., 2002), respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental design and citation to previous work

claim: Visual stimulation was performed in the photopic light regime that predominantly activates cone photoreceptors.
source: Visual stimulation was performed in the photopic light regime that predominantly activates cone photoreceptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental design

claim: The noise stimulus consisted of a center spot (37.5 degrees visual angle in diameter) and a surround annulus (approx. 120×90 degrees visual angle without the center spot).
source: The noise stimulus consisted of a center spot (37.5 degrees visual angle in diameter) and a surround annulus (approx. 120×90 degrees visual angle without the center spot) that simultaneously flickered in UV and green based on 5 Hz binary random sequences (Figure 1b)
evidence: Supported by experimental design

claim: Neuronal responses to parametric stimuli are easy to interpret and allow to systematically quantify chromatic RF properties of visual neurons.
source: Neuronal responses to such relatively simple, parametric stimuli are easy to interpret and allow to systematically quantify chromatic RF properties of visual neurons in the mouse (Szatko et al., 2020) and zebrafish retina (Zimmermann et al., 2018), as well as in primate V1 (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: There is extensive rod-cone opponency in mice, comparing signals from UV-sensitive cones in the ventral retina to rod signals.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated that there is extensive rod-cone opponency in mice, comparing signals from UV-sensitive cones in the ventral retina to rod signals (Szatko et al., 2020; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Rhim and Nauhaus, 2023; Khani and Gollisch, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Rod-cone opponency in the retina requires the integration across center and surround components of receptive fields.
source: In the retina, this mechanism relies on integrating information from cone signals in the RF center with rod signals in the RF surround (Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: There is evidence for rod-cone opponency in monochromatic humans.
source: Interestingly, there is also evidence for rod-cone opponency in monochromatic humans (Reitner et al., 1991)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: A neuronal circuit to compare rod and cone signals exists in other mammals as well.
source: suggesting that a neuronal circuit to compare rod and cone signals exists in other mammals as well
evidence: Inferred from evidence of rod-cone opponency in humans

claim: It is unclear to what extent behavioral color discrimination in mice is driven by rod-cone versus cone-cone comparisons.
source: At this point, it is still unclear to what extent behavioral color discrimination in mice (Denman et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2004) is driven by rod-cone versus cone-cone comparisons.
evidence: Acknowledged gap in current knowledge

claim: Rods likely contribute to the prominent color-opponent neuronal responses observed in mouse V1.
source: However, it is very likely that rods contribute to the prominent color-opponent neuronal responses we observed in mouse V1.
evidence: Inferred from experimental context and previous studies

claim: Cone-cone comparisons are challenging in posterior V1 due to the co-expression of S-opsin in M-cones.
source: This is especially true for posterior V1 receiving input from the ventral retina where cone-cone comparisons are challenging due to the co-expression of S-opsin in M-cones (Szél et al., 1992; Baden et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Color-opponency in posterior V1 is best explained by a model that compares S-opsin with Rhodopsin.
source: The involvement of rods in generating color-opponent responses is supported by retinal data (Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Joesch and Meister, 2016) and a recent study performed in mouse visual cortex showing that color-opponency in posterior V1 is best explained by a model that compares S-opsin with Rhodopsin (Rhim and Nauhaus, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: A neuronal substrate supporting color vision exists in both the upper and lower visual field.
source: suggesting that a neuronal substrate supporting color vision exists in both the upper and lower visual field
evidence: Inferred from distribution of color-opponent response types

claim: Color-opponency in the upper visual field could support threat detection.
source: As most predators are expected to approach the mouse from above, color-opponency in the upper visual field could well support threat detection.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on ecological considerations

claim: Color-opponent RF structures may result in a more reliable signal in visual scenes with inhomogeneous illumination.
source: Especially for visual scenes with inhomogeneous illumination (e.g. in the forest), which result in large intensity fluctuations at the photoreceptor array, color-opponent RF structures may result in a more reliable signal (discussed in Maximov, 2000; Kelber et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous discussions

claim: Objects in the sky, underwater, or in the snow are often more visible in the UV than the green wavelength range.
source: The dark object had a higher contrast in the UV than green channel, as it has been shown that objects in the sky (Qiu et al., 2021), underwater (Cronin and Bok, 2016; Losey et al., 1999), or in the snow (Tyler et al., 2014) are often more visible in the UV than the green wavelength range.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Functional neuron types in mouse V1 with distinct color properties unevenly sample different parts of the visual scene.
source: Our results suggest that functional neuron types in mouse V1 with distinct color properties unevenly sample different parts of the visual scene, and might thereby serve a distinct role in driving visually guided behavior like predator detection.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and modeling results

claim: The asymmetry in color processing across visual space matches the statistics of natural scenes experienced by mice.
source: Furthermore, we found that color-opponency is especially pronounced in posterior V1 that encodes the sky, matching the statistics of natural scenes experienced by mice.
evidence: Supported by comparison with natural scene statistics from previous studies

claim: The results support the hypothesis that neurons in the visual cortex asymmetrically represent information across the visual field, facilitating specific visual tasks such as the robust detection of aerial predators in noisy natural scenes.
source: The results of our study support the hypothesis that neurons in the visual cortex asymmetrically represent information across the visual field, facilitating specific visual tasks such as the robust detection of aerial predators in noisy natural scenes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results
